messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aroha is an eighty-year-old Māori woman who has spent most of her working life as a welder, a trade she took up in her fifties after her children were grown, finding in the precision and heat of the work a steadiness she had rarely felt elsewhere. She is married — her second marriage, to a man she describes as gentle — and it is partly the contrast with her first husband that makes the events of her past so difficult to revisit. For several years during her first marriage, Aroha was subjected to repeated physical violence by her then-partner: blows to the face and ribs, being thrown against walls, one occasion on which she lost consciousness on the kitchen floor and woke alone in the dark. She did not seek help at the time, telling herself and others that things were manageable, that she was strong. She left eventually, rebuilt her life with considerable determination, and for many years functioned well enough that the past seemed, if not resolved, at least contained. It was only in the last year, following a minor workplace injury that required surgery and a period of enforced rest, that the containment failed.

The surgery and recovery confronted Aroha with her body in ways she had long avoided. Lying still, dependent, she found herself revisiting the old injuries — not as memories exactly, but as a felt certainty that what had been done to her had left permanent damage that no surgeon could address. She had come to believe, with a quiet and unshakeable conviction, that her body had been broken in some fundamental way by her first husband, that its capacity to heal or to be trusted had been used up. This belief — that her body was unreliable, that she could no longer read its signals as honest — fed directly into a state of vigilance she struggled to name but could not escape. If her body could not be trusted, then the environment it inhabited had to be monitored constantly, because she could no longer rely on her own physical responses to warn her in time.

At home, which should have been the one place of safety, Aroha found herself perpetually on guard. Even in the house she shares with her husband — a man who has never raised a hand to her — she scanned rooms as she entered them, noted where exits were, startled at ordinary sounds. Nights became particularly difficult. She woke repeatedly, sometimes sitting upright in the dark to check that the room was as she had left it, listening for footsteps that were not there. Falling back to sleep after these checks was rarely possible; she would lie rigid, ears sharp, until the sky began to lighten. The exhaustion that accumulated across weeks of broken sleep deepened her sense of fragility, which in turn confirmed what she already feared: that she was permanently altered, that the woman who had once welded steel with steady hands and slept soundly was gone. The hypervigilance and the appraisals fed one another in a loop she could feel but could not interrupt — her certainty about her body's damage kept her nervous system at a pitch that felt like evidence of further damage, and the sleepless nights and constant alertness seemed only to prove that she would never again feel normal.

At the welding shop where she still works part-time, the physical demands of the job had become a source of dread rather than satisfaction. Each ache or tremor in her hands was read as confirmation that her body was failing her, that she could not trust what it told her. Colleagues noticed she had become quieter, more withdrawn; she had stopped taking on the longer shifts she once relished.

What finally brought Aroha to seek help was a conversation with her husband, who told her, carefully and with evident distress, that he was frightened for her — that she seemed to be disappearing. She came to the first session saying very little about what she hoped for, except that she wanted, someday, to sleep through the night in her own home without waking to check that she was still alive. What she feared most was that it was already too late — that whatever had been taken from her could not be returned.
